details:
**"The Red Wheelbarrow"**
Williams's most famous poem, a single sentence of 16 words split into four two-line stanzas of four words each: "so much depends / upon // a red wheel / barrow // glazed with rain / water // beside the white / chickens." It first appeared untitled as poem XXII in Spring and All and is a classic example of Imagism's focus on concrete objects.

**"This Is Just to Say"**
A 28-word poem written like a note left for his wife: "I have eaten / the plums / that were in / the icebox // and which / you were probably / saving / for breakfast // Forgive me / they were delicious / so sweet / and so cold." His wife Flossie wrote a joking "Reply" note, and Kenneth Koch parodied it in "Variations on a Theme by William Carlos Williams" ("I chopped down the house that you had been saving to live in next summer").

**Paterson**
Williams's five-book epic about Paterson, New Jersey, a city on the Passaic River, which he imagines as a sleeping giant: Paterson "lies on his right side, head near the thunder / of the waters filling his dreams!" (the Passaic Falls). Book One, "The Delineaments of Giants," contains his credo "Say it, no ideas but in things." Williams worked as a physician in nearby Rutherford, New Jersey, and was on staff at Passaic General Hospital.

**Spring and All**
Williams's 1923 collection mixing poems and prose, which includes "The Red Wheelbarrow," "To Elsie," and "The Rose" (whose petal's edge "cuts without cutting"). Its opening poem begins "By the road to the contagious hospital / under the surge of the blue / mottled clouds" and describes "patches of standing water / the scattering of tall trees." As "Lifeless in appearance, sluggish / dazed spring approaches," plants such as the "wildcarrot leaf" "enter the new world naked, / cold, uncertain of all," and finally "grip down and begin to awaken" with "the stark dignity of / entrance."

**"Danse Russe"**
A poem in which the speaker, while "my wife is sleeping / and the baby and Kathleen / are sleeping" and "the sun is a flame-white disc / in silken mists / above shining trees," dances "naked, grotesquely / before my mirror / waving my shirt round my head," singing "I am lonely." It ends "Who shall say I am not / the happy genius of my household?"

**"Asphodel, That Greeny Flower"**
A long late love poem to his wife Flossie, asking her forgiveness. It opens "Of asphodel, that greeny flower, / like a buttercup / upon its branching stem- / save that it's green and wooden," a flower said to grow in Hades. The speaker says "I come, my sweet, / to sing to you," notes that "All women are not Helen... / but have Helen in their hearts," and observes "It is difficult / to get the news from poems / yet men die miserably every day / for lack / of what is found there." It is written in his "triadic line" (variable foot), stepped tercets indented across the page.

**Pictures from Brueghel and Other Poems**
Williams's final collection (1962), which won the Pulitzer Prize after his death. Its title sequence has poems about paintings by the Flemish painter Pieter Brueghel the Elder, such as The Hunters in the Snow.

**"Landscape with the Fall of Icarus"**
A poem from Pictures from Brueghel about Brueghel's painting, in which a farmer keeps plowing while "unsignificantly / off the coast / there was / a splash quite unnoticed / this was / Icarus drowning."

**"The Dance"**
A poem describing Brueghel's painting The Kermess, in which "the dancers go round, they go round and / around," with "the squeal and the blare and the / tweedle of bagpipes" and peasants "kicking and rolling about." It begins and ends with the same line.

**"The Great Figure"**
A short poem in which the speaker, "Among the rain / and lights," sees "the figure 5 / in gold / on a red / firetruck" rushing "to gong clangs / siren howls / and wheels rumbling / through the dark city." It inspired Charles Demuth's painting I Saw the Figure 5 in Gold.

**"To Elsie"**
A poem from Spring and All that begins "The pure products of America / go crazy." It is about a troubled young woman working as a servant in the Williams household and the rural poverty she came from.

**"The Use of Force"**
A short story drawn from Williams's medical practice. A doctor examining a sick girl, Mathilda, must force open her mouth to check for diphtheria, and he is disturbed by the pleasure he takes in overpowering her resistance.

**White Mule**
Williams's 1937 novel, the first of a trilogy, about the immigrant Joe and Gurlie Stecher and their infant daughter Flossie in New York around 1900. The baby is said to kick like "white mule," a strong moonshine whiskey.

**"Portrait of a Lady"**
A love poem that opens "Your thighs are appletrees / whose blossoms touch the sky." The speaker keeps losing track of his images and asking himself, "Which sky?" and "Agh! what / sort of man was Fragonard?"

**"The Crowd at the Ball Game"**
A poem from Spring and All about a baseball crowd "moved uniformly / by a spirit of uselessness / which delights them." The crowd can turn menacing like a mob.
